summary.text: A carboxylic acid is a polar organic acid that contains a carboxyl group, −C(=O)−OH, attached to an R-group.
Carboxylic acids are often considered weak acids because they only partially ionise in water, and they donate protons (H⁺).
They occur widely, including amino acids and fatty acids, and are used to make polymers, pharmaceuticals, solvents and food additives.

facts.label: Water-soluble size
facts.value: Acids of 1 to 5 carbons dissolve in water

facts.label: Infrared band
facts.value: Sharp C=O band between 1680 and 1725 cm⁻¹

items.prompt: A carboxylic acid with an -ic acid name gives up a proton. How is the leftover anion usually named?

options.label: With the suffix -ate
With the suffix -oic
With the suffix -ane
With the suffix -yl

items.explain: The carboxylate anion is usually named with the suffix -ate, in keeping with the -ic acid and -ate pattern; acetate is the conjugate base of acetic acid.

items.prompt: A short-chain acid dissolves easily in water, but a much longer-chain acid barely does. Why?

options.label: The long chain makes the acid too heavy to mix with water at all
The long carbon chain adds hydrophobic character that grows with its length
The long chain holds fewer carboxyl groups, so it cannot be an acid
The long chain pulls water into dimers that settle out of solution

items.explain: Smaller acids dissolve in water, whereas bigger ones have limited solubility because the alkyl chain grows increasingly hydrophobic.

items.prompt: A hydrophobic carboxylic acid will not dissolve in water. A chemist adds aqueous sodium hydroxide. What happens?

options.label: It stays undissolved, since the base cannot reach it
It turns into a gas that bubbles out of the water
It reacts to give a water-soluble sodium salt
It forms a stronger acid that is harder to dissolve

items.explain: Aqueous sodium hydroxide reacts with carboxylic acids, even hydrophobic ones, to yield water-soluble sodium salts.

items.prompt: Why does it take more heat to boil a carboxylic acid than to boil water?

options.label: Its molecules are lighter, so they stay close to the liquid surface
Its molecules repel one another, so heat has to push them apart
Its molecules bond to water in the air, so boiling takes longer
Its molecules pair up through hydrogen bonds, and that pairing must be overcome

items.explain: Carboxylic acids form stabilized dimers through hydrogen bonds, so the dimer bonds must be broken or the whole pair vaporized, which raises the boiling requirements.

items.prompt: A perfumer wants a pleasant fruity scent from a sour-smelling acid. What kind of derivative should she look at?

options.label: Its esters
Its sodium salts, which are soaps
Its carboxylate anion in water
Its dimers in a nonpolar solvent

items.explain: Carboxylic acids often smell strongly sour, while their esters tend to have fruity, pleasant odours and many are used in perfume.

items.prompt: Carbonic acid, found in bicarbonate buffer systems, has a part that looks like a COOH group. Is it generally classed as a carboxylic acid?

options.label: Yes, because it has a COOH-style group
No, despite the look-alike group
Yes, because it donates protons
No, because it has no oxygen

items.explain: Carbonic acid is not generally classed as a carboxylic acid despite having a moiety that looks like a COOH group.
